President, distinguished delegates, ladies and gentlemen. The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela presents its annual report to the Human Rights Council pursuant to resolution 57/36. The report contains updates on the human rights situation in Venezuela from 1 September 2025 to to 31 July 2026. The report is accompanied by two session documents. The first examines developments in the main human rights violations that occur in the context of the mandate of the mission and the continuity of the repressive apparatus of the system. The second the so-called colectivos and their links with the state authorities, and the role of the colectivos. Both investigations are in line with the mandate of the council. In the reporting period, an extraordinary event occurred: the military intervention by the United States of America on 3 January, which led to the apprehension of President Maduro and opened a new political milestone in the country. The mission described that event as being contrary to international law. With respect to the reporting period between September and December 2025, the findings of the mission confirmed that human rights violations continued to take place at the same scale in line with patterns that are fully consistent with those that have been documented in previous reports. The change in Government and the political events that have occurred since 3 January have led to observable modifications in the human rights situation. The interim Government introduced changes in the cabinet the highest levels of the armed forces and within the structure and composition of the Supreme Court of Justice. They modified the political discourse, emphasizing messages of peace and national reconciliation, and adopted measures of political liberalization, which has reactivated public activity in Venezuela. The government opened a process of releases from prison which was covered by a new amnesty law that was adopted. Starting at the end of January, the mission detected a significant drop in arbitrary detentions on political grounds, especially those of longer duration, as well as enforced disappearances. The mission recognises that those qualitative changes have genuine consequences for many Venezuelan people and families. The names of the persons released have not been made public, and in the absence of transparent, verifiable data, the number of people released continues to be uncertain and subject to controversy. We estimate that between 800 and 1,000 people were released between 25 September and 26 August. The mission continues to document new arbitrary detentions from 3 January. There have been at least 17 in the first eight months of this year, according to our estimates. That represents a marked reduction compared with the same period last year. Nonetheless, it has been accompanied by an increase in short-term arbitrary detentions, where the authorities have recurred to as a form of intimidation against opposition or persons perceived as being opposition, including some who have who have long been subjected to longer detentions. That has particular resonance in the context of the widespread abuses that have been committed during the past decade, which constitute a powerful reminder to political activists and human rights defenders that their activities are being followed and that the repressive apparatus is still in place, despite significant releases of detainees in the past eight months. Hundreds of people continue to be arbitrarily deprived of freedom and subjected to tough conditions in centres where mistreatment and torture continue to be endemic. In the absence of public data, NGOs place up to 500 people detained on political grounds. That is a reminder of the the conditions between the elections of 2024. The mission is profoundly troubled about the situation regarding the possible continuity of systematic attacks against the population in the sense of article 7 of the Rome Statute of the ICC. Although certain violations have decreased, the mission continues to document cases of enforced disappearance and deaths of persons in detention, in custody since the 3rd of January. The mission in particular, is troubled by the persistence of torture in a number of detention centres in Venezuela. We are concerned in particular by facts that we have documented in the maximum security prison of Rodeo I and in the Forto Waipuro military prison, where the highest number of prisoners in detention on political grounds are kept. We have had extensive interviews with persons who have been released. That has allowed us to learn more about the frequency of the practice of torture and the nature and especially the special cruel practices and methods used, including methods that the mission had not previously documented. That is what we learned from those interviews. The central question in the mission report this year has been: "If the perceived changes in the political situation and the human rights situation have been accompanied by any change in the structures that made possible the repression for many years. Thus far, the mission has not found sufficient indicators of a genuine, sustainable break." when it comes to the government of Maduro and the patterns of repression that characterised that period. On the contrary, we noted that the structure of the repressive apparatus of the state has stayed completely intact. The persistence of the repressive apparatus is manifested in the continuity of the same legal framework that was used to coerce the autonomous functioning of operators in the civic and democratic space, in the lack of reform in police, security and intelligence services involved by action or omission in repression, in the lack of accountability for perpetrators of the gravest human rights violations and international crimes, in the continued restrictions on the functioning of civil society organisations, media and political parties, in the harassment that leaders and social activists continue to face, political leaders, and also in the ongoing surveillance and social control that the population is subjected to. Perhaps the best expression that the repressive apparatus is still intact and continues to affect decision making at the highest level is the continuance of the actors who perpetrated repression in the civil and military hierarchies. Uncertainty, which currently is present in the country, and the limited, easily reversible nature of the changes noted, is manifested in two events yesterday. One, the national communications commission announced, in the context of political dialogue between Government and Opposition, the formal restoration of access to various national and international media platforms. At the same time, we found out about the detention of Javier Ropesa, a former Opposition politician. He went into exile in 2024, returned to Venezuela and was He was released a few hours later. In the current cycle, the mission continued its investigations into armed civilian groups, these groups that are called colectivos. We have reasonable grounds to believe that those colectivos have supported repression through surveillance and through identifying objectives for repression, as well as through their participation in overseeing protests, in the security apparatus and in selective political repressions, in a climate of practically complete impunity. At the same time, the everyday presence within communities has allowed them to exercise other forms of control. Colectivos participate in the management and distribution of food, fuel, services and social benefits. They oversee political activities and mediate in conflicts, and that is done through coercion. The mission documented various forms of ties between the colectivos and the state, including public support from the highest authorities to those armed groups when it comes to resources and financing, the integration of members of the colectivos in public institutions and within security entities, and also the presence of officials or ex-officials within the colectivos themselves. The mission was able to conclude that there is an express and implicit overlap of functions related to public order and social control. The colectivos cannot be considered formal organs of the state. Nonetheless, the mission has reasonable grounds to conclude that certain conduct by members of the colectivos can be attributed to the state. Independent of attributing a concrete act, a state has an obligation to prevent abuses by those groups, should investigate acts, sanction perpetrators and ensure reparations for the victims. The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela today has an opportunity to move towards genuine change. sustainable change in the human rights situation and to make genuine progress in restoring the rule of law and democratic governance. What is needed is reform of institutions and laws that are linked to the political repression of the past decade. that the perpetrators of grave international violations should be brought duly to account before the justice system, and the victims should be recognized as such and receive compensation. I thank you.

Thank you.

Genuine co-operation should be able to recognise progress, generate trust and constructively support national efforts. Venezuela has adopted tangible measures that merit being considered objectively, the amnesty law for national reconciliation, democratic coexistence and peace, the program for peace and democratic coexistence, the judicial reform proceedings, application of non-custodial measures, which have benefited 8,743 people, and the on-going review of cases to address existing concerns. All that is in the context of the process of national political dialogue that guides the actions of the Venezuelan State. We trust that that progress can also be recognised and supported. Co-operation cannot be built on predetermined perceptions or through pronouncements that offer a piecemeal vision of the national reality. With respect to requests for access to detention centres, it is important to point out that Venezuela maintains fluid, constructive dialogue with the Red Cross. In the context of protocols agreed with national authorities, the Red Cross has been developing technical visits, providing cooperation and assistance with a feeling of humanity and dignity. That same logic that was shown after the earthquakes of 24 June through the Venezuela renaissance plan, with the support of the UN system, cooperation based on respect and national ownership can yield tangible results to protect rights and preserve human dignity even in the midst of tragedy. President, based on that conviction, Venezuela rejects any attempt to extend the mandate of the so-called International Independent Fact-Finding Mission. For almost seven years, that mechanism, established and extended without the consent or the cooperation of the Venezuelan state, has raised serious concerns as to its objectivity, impartiality and non-selectivity, key principles to avoid politicisation of human rights. After almost seven years, what concrete results has this structure yielded to improve promotion and protection of human rights in Venezuela? Has it generated better cooperation? Has it strengthened national capacities? Has it helped build trust? Our response is clear. Perpetuating confrontational mechanisms is no substitute for cooperation, nor does it bring us any closer to genuine solutions. These thoughts are all the more necessary given the grave financial crisis at the UN. It doesn't seem reasonable to continue attributing increasingly scarce resources to structures that undermine existing institutional mechanisms. And also, we shouldn't ignore the impact of UCMs on the full enjoyment of human rights of the Venezuelan people. Venezuela aspires to a multilateral system of human rights that's robust, credible and effective. We believe the time has come to move towards the conclusion, the closure of this mechanism to prevent its indefinite perpetuation. Therefore, we make a call to members of this organ not to support any further extension of the mandate of the so-called International Fact-Finding Mission. Instead, we should move towards the orderly closure of this mechanism, preferring, rather, the UPR, technical cooperation, genuine dialogue and universal mechanisms able to effectively support states and yield tangible results in the field of human rights. The Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela reaffirms its will to work with the international community on the basis of mutual respect, sovereign equality and non-intervention. Cooperation requires trust. Trust is built through respect, objectivity and dialogue. That is the path that our country offers and that it is ready to continue moving there. Thank you.

Thank you.

Mr. Vice President, the European Union thanks the Fact-Finding Mission for its report and reiterate its full support for its mandate. We urge Venezuela to engage constructively with all human rights mechanisms and to grant the FFM access to the country and ensure the continued presence of OHCHR.

The EU remains concerned by the human rights

situation in Venezuela and by reports of ongoing repression, including against political actors, civil society, human rights defenders, and independent media. We're also concerned by the role of so-called colectivos in violence and repression, as well as the collaboration between these organizations and the authorities. The EU regrets Venezuela's withdrawal from the Rome Statute and calls on it to remain a state party

to the International Criminal Court.

The EU welcomes the release of political prisoners, while regretting that many of those released remain subject to restrictions. We call on the authorities to release all remaining political prisoners unconditionally and to dismantle the repressive security apparatus. We reaffirm our solidarity with the Venezuelan people following the June earthquakes. We support an inclusive, Venezuelan-led dialogue for a democratic transition that restores democracy, the rule of law, and human rights. Ms. Macha, what steps should the Venezuelan authorities take to facilitate the restoration of democratic institutions? I thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Luxembourg on behalf of a group of countries.

In particular, we are deeply concerned about the cases of Veronica Sanchez, Oswaldo Castillo, Rolando Guevara, Franklin Duran, and many others. We call for the immediate and unconditional release and for the prompt release of all persons arbitrarily detained. While we welcome the ongoing dialogue between the Venezuelan authorities and representatives of the 2015 National Assembly, including its focus on the judicial system, press freedom, and the rule of law, we urge the authorities to restore civic space, press freedom, and inclusive political processes by ensuring the full participation of all political and civic actors in Venezuela, including women, youth, and marginalized communities. We appreciate the authorities' technical cooperation agenda with the ICRC on detention centres and encourage them also to cooperate fully with the fact-finding mission. Changes on the ground make their independent monitoring for accountability all the more important. Therefore, we strongly support the extension of the mandate. We reaffirm our solidarity with the Venezuelan people following the devastating June earthquakes.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Chile.

Thank you, Vice-President. Chile thanks the International Independent Fact-Finding Mission for its report, and we recognise the importance of this mandate for documenting violations and contributing to accountability in the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela. We've taken note of the release of many political prisoners and the reduction of long prison sentences and the opening up of space for civil society. those are positive steps nevertheless this has not been accompanied by sustained institutional reforms there are hundreds of people who arbitrarily detained they're exposed to torture ill treatment they don't have medical treatment and their prison conditions are not in line with international standards there are patterns of repression which continue and there is a lack of investigation and accountability. In the same vein, we're worried about the findings on the Colectivos, their links to state authorities and their intimidation, attacks on opposition figures, journalists and human rights defenders, as well as repression of demonstrations. We support your recommendations, notably the release of those arbitrarily detained, hold investigations, reform institutions which have been involved and strengthen cooperation with international human rights mechanisms. Thank you very much.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Paraguay.

Thank you, Vice President. We thank the mission for presenting its report, as well as the updated information on the human rights situation in Venezuela and the progress made. We reiterate the importance of ensuring full respect for human rights and the will of the Venezuelan people. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Brazil.

Brazil also welcomes the start of the dialogue between the government and certain sectors of the opposition. We encourage this to be continued. We believe it's important to follow up on measures such as the programme for peaceful and democratic coexistence as well as fully restoring the office of the High Commissioner for Human Rights in the country. There must be legal institutional reforms such as bringing laws on NGOs and the constitutional law on hatred in line with international human rights standards. We regret Venezuela's decision to withdraw from the Rome Statute and We are concerned about the effects of unilateral coercive measures on the human rights situation in the country. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Colombia.

Thank you, Vice-President. Colombia would like to thank the mission for its update, and we've taken careful note of the presentation's conclusions. This must cover all persons in detention, including Colombian nationals who are being held incommunicado. Thank you.

Therefore we welcome the authorities attempts to reduce the degree of opposition with the political opposition to achieve political stability, inclusivity and protect the rights and freedoms of citizens. Thank you.

Human rights cannot be advanced by creating additional political confrontation, nor should the Council become an instrument for exerting pressure on governments that pursue independent national policies. Eritrea therefore encourages engagement with Venezuela on the basis of sovereign equality and mutual respect, while recognizing the primary responsibility of national institutions for addressing human rights challenges. Eritrea further believes that the Human Rights Council should prioritize constructive cooperation and technical assistance where requested and mutually agreed, rather than mechanisms that risk becoming instruments of political pressure. Their trial therefore calls for an approach based on dialogue rather than confrontation, cooperation rather than coercion, and universal principles rather than selected country targeting. I thank you, Mr. President.

Thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you, Vice-President. Uruguay would like to thank the Mission for presenting its reports, and we reiterate how important this mandate is. We're worried about information according to which hundreds of people continue to be arbitrarily detained, and the persistent reports of torture, ill treatment, and prison conditions which fell well short of human rights obligations. We believe that there should be effective investigations and accountability for serious violations. There must be freedom for civic space, fundamental freedoms and independent judicial system. Democratic reform must be achieved peacefully, inclusively, and with full respect for the will of the Venezuelan people and human rights in line with the United Nations Charter and international law. Thank you.

Thank you.

Moreover, imposing parallel mechanisms on a state that is already cooperating with the established frameworks creates an unnecessary burden on the multilateral system, particularly at a time when resource rationalization is paramount. It is imperative that this Council remains guided by its founding principles of universality, impartiality, objectivity and non-selectivity. Progress requires peaceful, domestically driven, democratic processes free from externally imposed mechanisms. To conclude, Sri Lanka calls upon the Council to prioritise genuine partnership with Venezuelan authorities, as this remains the most effective avenue to safeguard and advance the rights of its people. Thank you.

Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Italy.

Thank you, Mr. Vice-President.

As a party to the European Union statement, Italy reaffirms its strong support for the work of the fact-finding.

Mission, whose effectiveness on the ground is an essential prerequisite to ensure accountability.

We encourage Venezuela to engage constructively with human rights mechanisms and to grant them complete and unhindered access to the country, also allowing the Office of the High Commissioner to fully operate.

We welcome the recent.

Releases of political prisoners and stress the need to ensure complete and unconditional release of all political prisoners and those arbitrarily detained. Italy calls on Venezuela to respect all human rights and fundamental.

Freedoms, including the rights of peaceful assembly, association and freedom.

Of expression, and those of political opposition, human rights defenders and representatives of independent media and civil society. Thank you.

I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Greece.

Its implementation should be prompt, transparent, and non-discriminatory, consistent with international human rights obligations. All those arbitrarily detained for political reasons should be released. We encourage the government to build on these steps and accelerate reform and democratization through meaningful, sustained dialogue with the opposition, with the participation of civil society. This dialogue should deliver an agreed roadmap with concrete measures and clear timelines to strengthen the rule of law, safeguard fundamental freedoms, and create the conditions for credible, inclusive elections. Continuing reports of repression and restrictions on freedom of expression remain deeply concerning. Political actors, journalists, and human rights defenders must be able to operate freely and without fear. Accountability for human rights violations and respect for victims' rights are essential to lasting reconciliation. Greece supports a peaceful, inclusive and Venezuelan-led democratic process.
I give the floor to the distinguished representative of Peru.

Thank you, Vice-President. Peru would like to thank the Mission for presenting its report. Thank you.

Thank you.

Thank you.

This was the last speaker we could accommodate at this meeting. Excellencies, dear participants, I understand that certain delegations have requested to exercise the right of reply. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Rwanda. You have three minutes.

Thank you. My delegation took note and would like to take the floor to refute the unfounded allegations made against Rwanda by the delegation of Burundi and the Democratic Republic of Congo. Assertions made before this Council should be supported by verifiable facts, particularly when addressing a conflict involving multiple States, armed groups and other actors. It is important to recall that Burundi is itself a direct military actor in the eastern DRC. Burundian forces remain deployed in South Sudan and have participated in South Kivu and have participated in military operation alongside the Congolese armed forces. And the coalition, it has been documented. It's created with the Front Democratique de Liberation du Rwanda, the FDLR, and the Wazalendo militia. This involvement has been documented by independent reporting and cannot be overlooked when discussing responsibility for the continuing hostilities. The intensification of military operations in South Kivu, including the use of drones, aircraft and heavy weapons, has placed civilian population at considerable risk. Rather than advancing selective accusations, this Council should insist on credible, verifiable of the conduct of all parties and accountability for violations committed against civilians. Rwanda calls against attempts to deflect responsibility for the complex security and human rights situation in the eastern DRC. The presence and activities of numerous armed groups, foreign forces and other armed actors must form part of any credible assessment on the situation. Burundi should focus on addressing the human rights concern within its own jurisdiction, including strengthening the human rights provided for all its citizens. The Democratic Republic of Congo should contribute constructively to the implementation of existing peace commitment, including the Washington Framework, and refrain from undermining these efforts. Burundi should address the human rights concern with its own jurisdiction, including provide equal protection and opportunities for all citizens. Rwanda remains committed to regional peace. Allegations should not substitute for evidence, nor should this Council be used to obstruct the responsibility of actors directly engaged in the conflict. I thank you.

Thank you.
